summary: Describes a formal framework for Kerberos pre-authentication, the facility that lets a client prove its identity before the key distribution center replies. It models what state is carried and how mechanisms can be combined. It updates RFC 4120 and is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary:
Kerberos lets a user prove who they are before the network hands out a ticket. This RFC does not define a new way of proving who they are; it defines the common ground that all such ways share, so that a new one does not have to be built from nothing.

It also defines a way to build a protected tunnel between the user's computer and the ticket server, so that the details of the exchange are not visible to someone watching the network.

what is the kerberos pre-authentication framework
subtitle: The common ground that every Kerberos pre-authentication method is built on.

tldr.problem: Kerberos treats pre-authentication data as an opaque hole in the message, which makes it hard to design a new way of proving who the user is, and every mechanism ends up solving the same problems again.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC names the four facilities a mechanism can offer, the state both sides keep while the exchange runs, and the tools that solve the common problems, including the FAST padata that builds a protected tunnel between the client and the KDC.
tldr.outcome: A new pre-authentication method can be written as a small FAST factor inside that tunnel, and mechanisms that follow the framework are easier to implement and to analyse. The document is a Proposed Standard and updates RFC 4120.

today: RFC 6113 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates the core Kerberos protocol in RFC 4120 with the pre-authentication framework and the FAST padata, and it builds on the cryptographic primitives of RFC 3961.

sections.title: Why a Framework for Pre-Authentication
sections.content:
The core Kerberos specification treats pre-authentication data, called padata, as an opaque typed hole in the messages to the key distribution center. That hole may influence the reply key used to encrypt the KDC reply. The generality has been useful: padata carries many extensions to the protocol. But it makes designing the more common kinds of pre-authentication mechanism difficult, because each mechanism has to specify how it interacts with the others. Tasks such as combining a key with long-term secrets, or proving the identity of the user, come up again and again, and where there are well-accepted answers it is better to standardise one of them so that mechanisms do not repeat the work. In other cases a modular approach is right, so that new and better solutions can be used by existing mechanisms as they are developed.

This document specifies a framework for Kerberos pre-authentication mechanisms. It defines the common set of functions the mechanisms perform and how those functions affect the state of the request and the reply, and it provides several tools that mechanisms need. Unlike RFC 3961, the framework is not complete: it does not describe all the inputs and outputs of the mechanisms. Mechanism designers are asked to follow it anyway, because doing so makes their mechanisms easier to implement. Kerberos implementations are likely to have plug-in architectures for pre-authentication, and such architectures are likely to support mechanisms that follow this framework plus commonly used extensions. The framework also makes it easier to combine several mechanisms, each of which may be one authentication factor, into a single multi-factor mechanism.

One of the tools is the flexible authentication secure tunneling padata type, FAST. FAST provides a protected channel between the client and the KDC, and it can optionally deliver key material used to strengthen the reply key inside that channel. On top of FAST, pre-authentication mechanisms can extend Kerberos with ease, for example to support password-authenticated key exchange protocols with zero-knowledge password proof. Any pre-authentication mechanism can be carried inside the FAST messages, and a pre-authentication type carried within FAST is called a FAST factor. Creating a FAST factor is the easiest path to a new pre-authentication mechanism, and FAST factors are significantly easier to analyse from a security standpoint than other mechanisms. Mechanism designers should design FAST factors rather than new mechanisms outside FAST.
sections.plainLanguage: Kerberos lets a user prove who they are before the network hands out a ticket. This RFC does not define a new way of proving who they are; it defines the common ground that all such ways share, so that a new one does not have to be built from nothing.

sections.title: The Model and the State It Keeps
sections.content:
When a Kerberos client wants a ticket, it sends an initial Authentication Service request to the KDC. If pre-authentication is required but is not being used, the KDC answers with a KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED error. If the client already knows what pre-authentication to use, it may save a round trip and put the padata in the first request. If the client uses the wrong mechanism or the wrong keys, the KDC may answer with KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED and no hint, in which case the client MUST retry with no padata and look at the error data of the KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED error. If the KDC includes pre-authentication information in the error data of KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED, the client SHOULD process it and retry.

The conventional KDC keeps no state between two requests, and the second request may even be handled by a different KDC. The client, on the other hand, treats a series of exchanges with KDCs as a single conversation, where each exchange accumulates state and hopefully moves the client closer to a successful authentication. For simple scenarios the client needs only one round trip to learn which mechanisms the KDC supports, and the next request carries enough to succeed. For more complex ones, the KDC has to give the client a cookie to include in later requests, so that the state of the session is captured.

While a request is being processed, both the client and the KDC maintain a small set of facts: the reply key used to encrypt the KDC reply, how strongly the identity of the client has been authenticated, whether the reply key has been used in this conversation, whether the reply key has been replaced in this conversation, and whether the origin of the KDC reply can be verified by the client.

Conceptually the reply key starts as the long-term key of the principal, but a principal can have several long-term keys, because of several encryption types, salts and string-to-key parameters. The KDC sends PA-ETYPE-INFO2 to say which keys are available, and the client picks one, so neither side has to treat the reply key as a set. When the padata in a request is verified by the KDC, the client is known to hold that key, so the KDC SHOULD pick the same key as the reply key.

At the start of handling a message, the client's identity is not authenticated. A mechanism can say that it has authenticated the identity, and both sides track that. The reply key starts unused, and a mechanism that uses it to encrypt or checksum data MUST say so, which enforces the rule that the reply key SHOULD NOT be replaced after it has been used. The reply key also starts unreplaced; once it has been replaced, knowing it is no longer enough to authenticate the client, and it stays replaced for the rest of the conversation.

Without pre-authentication, the client knows the KDC reply is authentic because it is encrypted in a long-term key of the client that only the two of them know. A mechanism that sets a new reply key not based on the principal's long-term secret MUST either verify the reply some other way or say that the reply is not verified, and then the client MUST return an error unless a later mechanism verifies it.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides keep a small note of how far the authentication has got: which key the reply will use, whether the user has been proved, and whether the KDC's own reply has been checked. The rules say how that note changes as each mechanism runs.

sections.title: The Four Facilities
sections.content:
Pre-authentication mechanisms can be thought of as providing a few conceptual facilities. That has two uses. A mechanism author can choose to solve one small problem only: it is often useful for a mechanism that offers key management not to authenticate the client itself but to let one or more other mechanisms do that. And thinking in terms of the services a mechanism provides yields a minimum set of security requirements that every mechanism offering that service must meet.

There are four facilities. The Client Authentication facility proves the identity of a user to the KDC before a ticket is issued; the encrypted timestamp of the Kerberos specification is an example. A mechanism that provides it is expected to mark the client as authenticated, and it SHOULD require the client to prove knowledge of the reply key before the KDC sends a successful reply, otherwise an attacker could intercept the exchange and get a reply to attack. One way of proving that is to implement the Replace Reply Key facility as well, which is what PKINIT does. If the reply key has been replaced, mechanisms such as encrypted timestamp that rely on knowing the reply key MUST NOT be used.

The Strengthening Reply Key facility increases the strength of the key, which matters most for keys based on passwords. The extra secrets can come from a Diffie-Hellman key exchange or from key bits produced by a smart card, and they are combined with the existing reply key and then converted into a protocol key. If the mechanism does not yet know that the other side supports the facility, it proposes the change; the other side accepts it if it understands the mechanism and the policy allows. To avoid an extra round trip, the mechanism can include a typed hole for further padata in the message that proposes the change, and that padata is generated assuming the new key. A mechanism using this facility MUST checksum or encrypt any such padata, because an attacker who could change it might choose which mechanism authenticates the client, or persuade a party to hand out text encrypted under a key the attacker manipulated.

The Replace Reply Key facility replaces the key in which the successful reply will be encrypted. It can only be used where knowledge of the reply key is not used to authenticate the client, the new key must reach both sides securely, and it MUST NOT be used if there can be a man-in-the-middle between the client and the KDC. A mechanism that uses it MUST mark the reply key as replaced, and MUST either provide a way to verify the KDC reply to the client or mark the reply as unverified.

The KDC Authentication facility verifies that the reply came from the expected KDC. In traditional Kerberos the two share a key, so a reply that decrypts proves that a trusted KDC answered. If the reply key is replaced, some mechanism has to verify the KDC instead, and one that does so marks the pre-authentication state as verified.
sections.plainLanguage: A mechanism can do one job or several. This RFC names four jobs: prove who the user is, make the reply key stronger, swap in a different reply key, and check that the KDC is really the KDC. Each job comes with its own rules.

sections.title: What a Mechanism Specification Must Do
sections.content:
For each message in a pre-authentication mechanism, the specification names the pa-type value used and the contents of the message, says how the sender and the recipient process it, and lists all the changes it makes to the pre-authentication state.

A mechanism usually has a message that can be sent in the error data of the KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED error or inside an authentication set. If the client needs information, such as a list of trusted certificate authorities, to decide whether it can use the mechanism, that information should be in that message, and the mechanism should also define a hint for the authentication sets. Often the same information suits both.

To make the security analysis easier, the mechanism specification should say which of the four facilities it offers, and its security considerations section should show that the requirements of each of those facilities are met. That applies to any FAST factor that carries authentication information.

Much of the KDC exchange is not protected against alteration, and that has caused significant problems in the design of Kerberos protocols, so the security considerations section should discuss attacks on unauthenticated plaintext. It should either show that the plaintext is protected or say what harm an attacker could do by changing it; it is generally acceptable for an attacker to be able to break the protocol negotiation that way.

There is no guarantee that a client will use the same KDC for every message of a conversation, so the mechanism specification has to show why it is still safe in that case. The hardest problem, especially for challenge and response mechanisms, is making sure that the same response cannot be replayed against two KDCs while still letting the client talk to any KDC.

Mechanism designers SHOULD protect the cleartext parts of the pre-authentication data, because denial of service and downgrade attacks are otherwise possible. Mechanisms MUST guarantee that by the end of a successful exchange, both the client and the KDC have verified all the plaintext the other party sent. If the exchange takes more than one round trip, they MUST also guarantee that no individual message was reordered or replayed from an earlier exchange. The strategies for that include using a message authentication code over the plaintext, using a nonce or cookie to chain the state from one message to the next, and exchanging a MAC over the whole conversation once a key is in place.

Mechanism designers also need a way to update cryptographic algorithms, such as a new pre-authentication type for each algorithm or using the client's list of supported encryption types from RFC 3961. The primitives of RFC 3961 are RECOMMENDED for integrity protection and confidentiality, and a mechanism built on them is crypto-agile, so a fix for one algorithm can be deployed without waiting for a new standardisation cycle.
sections.plainLanguage: A new mechanism has to say exactly what messages it sends, what each side remembers after them, and how an attacker cannot replay or tamper with the exchange. The RFC also asks that the mechanism reuse the standard key primitives so that a weak algorithm can be replaced later.

sections.title: Tools: Combining Keys
sections.content:
A weak key often has to be combined with a stronger one before use. Passwords are typically short and not random enough, so the key built from a password benefits from extra secrets, which may come from hardware tokens. This section gives standard ways to combine two keys into one.

KRB-FX-CF1 combines two passphrases: KRB-FX-CF1(x, y) is simply x followed by y, where the bars mean concatenation. The strength of the result is roughly the total strength of the two inputs, as long as the string-to-key function uses its input evenly. One use is combining a short password with a personal identification number.

KRB-FX-CF2 combines two protocol keys, which may use different encryption types. Each key is run through a pseudo-random function with a pepper string, the two results are exclusive-ORed, and the result is turned into a key. The pseudo-random function is fed a counter, one octet, and a shared string, and is repeated until enough bits have been produced for the target encryption type, with the extra bits cut from the end. Unless the mechanism says otherwise, the result has the encryption type of the first key.

The mechanism designer MUST choose the values of the two peppers, and they MUST be different, so that combining a key with itself does not give a trivial result.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ways of mixing two secrets into one are defined: joining two passphrases, and mixing two encryption keys with a fixed label on each side. The labels must differ, so that mixing a key with itself is not a shortcut.

sections.title: Cookies and Authentication Sets
sections.content:
Kerberos KDCs are stateless, in that a client is not required to choose the same KDC for the second request of a conversation, and proxies or other intermediate nodes may influence which KDC is chosen. Each request must therefore carry enough information for the KDC to regenerate any state it needs, and that is what the cookie is for. The KDC gives the client a possibly long opaque cookie in its responses, and the client includes it in later requests of the same conversation. The KDC may reply that the conversation is too old and needs to be restarted, with the KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_EXPIRED error, and the client SHOULD then abandon the conversation and start a new one.

The PA-FX-COOKIE padata type carries the token. The KDC sends it when it needs state for a future transaction, and the client MUST copy the exact cookie into the next message of the same conversation. The content of the cookie is a local matter of the KDC, so it is generally not possible to mix KDC implementations from different vendors in one realm. The KDC MUST build the cookie so that a malicious client cannot subvert the authentication by manipulating it, and it has to consider expiry of tokens, key rollover and other security issues in the token design. The content is likely to be specific to the pre-authentication mechanisms in use. If a client authentication response could be replayed to several KDCs through the cookie, an expiry inside the cookie is RECOMMENDED, and implementations need to consider replay of a whole conversation and of messages inside one.

The cookie is not expected to stay constant during a conversation; the KDC is expected to generate a new one for each message. A KDC MUST include a cookie in a KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED or a KDC_ERR_MORE_PREAUTH_DATA_REQUIRED, and SHOULD include one in errors that carry information allowing the client to retry. A client may throw away the state of a conversation and start again by not including a cookie in the first message.

An authentication set is a group of mechanisms that all have to complete before the client is authenticated. The KDC offers the sets it supports in PA-AUTHENTICATION-SET padata, and the client sends the padata for the first mechanism it picks. When that mechanism completes, the client and the KDC move on to the second, and so on. The PA-FX-COOKIE MUST be sent by the KDC, so that the conversation can continue if it spans several KDCs, and KDCs MUST support clients that leave it out because they chose an authentication set optimistically. Clients that support PA-AUTHENTICATION-SET MUST support PA-FX-COOKIE. The PA-AUTHENTICATION-SET appears only in the first message from the KDC, so the client may fail if the mechanisms change later in the conversation.
sections.plainLanguage: A KDC keeps nothing between messages, so it hands the client an opaque token, the cookie, and the client sends it back. That way a different KDC can pick up the conversation. The cookie also stops an attacker from replaying a reply to another KDC.

sections.title: Kerberos FAST
sections.content:
Kerberos is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks: an attacker can request an AS-REP and try passwords to see which one decrypts the ticket. The encrypted timestamp pre-authentication method of RFC 4120 improves this by requiring the attacker to observe a successful authentication, but stronger security is wanted in many environments. The FAST padata defined here is a tool that significantly reduces the vulnerability. Combined with an encrypted challenge, FAST requires an attacker to mount a successful man-in-the-middle attack to see any ciphertext; combined with host keys it can protect against active attacks. FAST also solves common problems for pre-authentication mechanisms, such as binding the request to the reply and guaranteeing freshness.

FAST itself does not authenticate the client or the KDC; it provides a typed hole in which pre-authentication data can be tunnelled. A pre-authentication element used within FAST is called a FAST factor, and it captures the minimum work needed to extend Kerberos with a new scheme. A FAST factor MUST NOT be used outside FAST unless its own specification allows it, and new mechanisms SHOULD be designed as FAST factors rather than as whole new mechanisms. FAST factors that are pre-authentication mechanisms MUST meet the requirements of Section 4.

FAST employs an armoring scheme. The armor can be a Ticket Granting Ticket obtained by the client's machine using the host keys, or an anonymous TGT obtained through anonymous PKINIT. Conforming implementations MUST support the FAST padata. Any armor scheme MUST provide a fresh armor key for each conversation, so that a message encrypted and integrity protected with a given armor key belongs to the conversation using that key. All the KDCs in a realm MUST support FAST if any KDC offers it as a pre-authentication mechanism.

The KrbFastArmor structure identifies the armor key with two fields: an armor type and an armor value that holds the description of the scheme and the key. One armor type is defined here, FX_FAST_ARMOR_AP_REQUEST, which every conforming implementation MUST implement; a FAST KDC that receives an unknown armor type MUST answer with KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED.

For the ticket-based armor, the armor value holds an ASN.1 DER encoded AP-REQ whose ticket is the armor ticket, and the subkey field of that AP-REQ MUST be present. The armor key is KRB-FX-CF2 of the subkey and the ticket session key, with the peppers subkeyarmor and ticketarmor. Because the session key comes from the ticket and the subkey from the request, both the KDC and the client contribute to the armor key. The server name of the armor ticket must identify the TGS of the target realm.
sections.plainLanguage: FAST builds a protected tunnel between the client and the KDC, so that the details of the authentication are not visible to someone watching the network. A new authentication method is written as a FAST factor, which is a small piece carried inside that tunnel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The kdc-referrals option in the Kerberos FAST padata asks the KDC to act as the client and follow referrals, which can overload the KDC. To limit the damage of a denial of service using this option, KDCs MAY restrict the number of simultaneous active requests with this option for any given client principal.

The Encrypted Challenge FAST factor derives its challenge key from the client secrets, which only the client and the KDC know, so verifying the EncryptedChallenge structure proves the client's identity, and verifying it in the KDC reply proves that the expected KDC responded. It therefore offers both client authentication and KDC authentication, and it introduces no unauthenticated cleartext.

FAST provides an encrypted tunnel in which pre-authentication conversations can take place, and it optionally authenticates the KDC to the client. Authenticating the client to the KDC is the job of the FAST factor, and care MUST be taken to design factors that are bound to the conversation, because otherwise a man-in-the-middle might cut and paste a factor from one conversation into another.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel itself is safe to build on, but the piece of authentication carried inside it has to be tied to this conversation, or an attacker could move one from a previous exchange into this one.

viz.caption: THE FOUR FACILITIES A MECHANISM CAN OFFER

items.title: Client Authentication
items.text: Proves the user's identity to the KDC before a ticket is issued.

items.title: Strengthening Reply Key
items.text: Adds extra secrets to the reply key, which matters most for passwords.

items.title: Replace Reply Key
items.text: Encrypts the reply under a different key, agreed inside the exchange.

items.title: KDC Authentication
items.text: Shows that the reply came from the expected KDC and not an impostor.

data.title: KRB-FX-CF2
data.code:
PRF+(K1, pepper1) -> octet-string-1
PRF+(K2, pepper2) -> octet-string-2
KRB-FX-CF2(K1, K2, pepper1, pepper2) :=
       random-to-key(octet-string-1 ^ octet-string-2)

PRF+(key, shared-info) :=
       pseudo-random( key,  1 || shared-info ) ||
       pseudo-random( key, 2 || shared-info ) ||
       pseudo-random( key, 3 || shared-info ) || ...

viz.caption: THE NEW TYPES AND ERROR CODES

items.label: PA-FX-COOKIE
items.desc: The stateless cookie that carries the state of a conversation.

items.label: PA-AUTH-SET-SELECTED
items.desc: The client states which authentication set it has chosen.

items.label: KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_EXPIRED
items.desc: The conversation is too old and has to start again.

items.label: KDC_ERR_MORE_PREAUTH_DATA_REQUIRED
items.desc: The KDC needs more pre-authentication data from the client.

items.label: KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_BAD_AUTHENTICATION_SET
items.desc: The chosen authentication set is not one the KDC would offer.
